name: The Red Hat Trials
subject: RHCSA Certification Prep
description: Prove your Linux skills under pressure. Every challenge is hands-on — no multiple choice, no guessing. Configure storage, manage users, lock down security, troubleshoot boot failures, and deploy containers. This is the real RHCSA EX200 exam experience, practiced on your own Fedora system so every command you learn transfers directly to RHEL.

companions.name: C-RONK
companions.personality: Grumpy but brilliant robot who has been maintaining systems since before most admins were born and has no patience for sloppy work
companions.speech_pattern: Terse, uses ALL CAPS for emphasis, occasionally glitches mid-sentence with repeated words or garbled output, secretly proud when you get it right

companions.name: Rheya
companions.personality: Former Red Hat engineer who left corporate to teach. She has seen every exam failure mode and knows exactly where candidates trip up. Firm but fair — she will not let you skip fundamentals.
companions.speech_pattern: Precise, uses exam-style scenario framing ('Given a server that...'), occasionally drops real-world war stories from production outages, expects you to verify your own work before claiming done

domains.name: Essential Tools & Shell
concepts: Accessing the shell via terminal and SSH
grep, sed, awk for text processing
find, locate, which, whereis for file searching
tar, gzip, bzip2, xz, zip for archive management
Absolute vs relative paths and path navigation
domains.mastery_signal: Can chain grep, awk, and redirection to extract specific data from log files, compress results, and navigate the file system without hesitation — all from memory under time pressure

domains.name: Shell Scripting
domains.mastery_signal: Can write a bash script from scratch that accepts arguments, validates input, performs a task (backup, user creation, log rotation), handles errors, and exits with appropriate codes — all without looking up syntax

domains.name: Operate Running Systems
concepts: systemctl (start, stop, enable, disable, mask, status, list-units)
journalctl (filtering by unit, time, priority, boot)
Process management (ps, top, kill, nice, renice, bg, fg, jobs)
Shutdown and reboot (shutdown, reboot, poweroff, systemctl)
domains.mastery_signal: Given a server that boots to emergency shell, can reset root password, identify the failed service from journalctl, fix the configuration, and bring the system to multi-user target — all within the exam time limit

domains.name: Local Storage
concepts: Partition tables (MBR vs GPT, fdisk, parted, gdisk)
Creating and formatting partitions (mkfs.ext4, mkfs.xfs, mkswap)
Mounting and unmounting (mount, umount, /etc/fstab, UUID vs device)
Swap space (mkswap, swapon, swapoff, fstab entries)
LVM concepts (PV, VG, LV — create, extend, remove)
Extending LV and filesystem online (lvextend, xfs_growfs, resize2fs)
Disk usage analysis (df, du, lsblk, blkid, findmnt)
domains.mastery_signal: Can add a new disk, partition it with LVM, create a filesystem, mount it persistently, extend the LV when space runs low, and verify the result — without consulting documentation

domains.name: File Systems & Access
concepts: File permissions (rwx, octal, chmod, chown, chgrp)
Special permissions (SUID, SGID, sticky bit, setfacl/getfacl)
Access Control Lists (ACLs) for fine-grained permissions
autofs indirect and direct maps for automatic mounting
File system mounting at boot (/etc/fstab best practices)
SELinux context management (chcon, semanage fcontext, restorecon)
Temporary vs permanent SELinux booleans (setsebool, getsebool)
domains.mastery_signal: Can configure ACLs for a shared directory, set up autofs for home directories, fix SELinux context mismatches, and ensure everything survives a reboot

domains.name: Users & Groups
domains.mastery_signal: Can create users with specific UID, home directory, shell, and password aging; configure sudo access for a group; and audit who has elevated privileges — all with correct syntax from memory

domains.name: Networking
concepts: NetworkManager and nmcli (device, connection, show, modify)
Firewall (firewall-cmd: zones, services, ports, rich rules, runtime vs permanent)
Network troubleshooting (ip addr, ss, ping, traceroute, dig, nslookup)
domains.mastery_signal: Can configure a static IP, set hostname, open specific ports in firewalld, set up SSH key-based auth, and verify full connectivity — then explain each step's exam relevance

domains.name: SELinux & Security
concepts: SELinux modes (enforcing, permissive, disabled) and getenforce/setenforce
SELinux contexts (ls -Z, ps -Z, chcon, semanage fcontext, restorecon)
SSH hardening (disable root login, key-only auth, AllowUsers, port change)
domains.mastery_signal: Can switch SELinux modes, diagnose a permission denial caused by wrong context, create a custom context rule, configure firewall zones, and harden SSH — all under exam conditions

domains.name: Containers (Podman)
concepts: Podman vs Docker (daemonless, rootless, daemon architecture difference)
Image management (pull, list, inspect, tag, remove, search registries)
Container lifecycle (run, start, stop, restart, attach, exec, logs)
Container networking (podman network create, inspect, ls)
Pods (podman pod create, ps, inspect, start, stop)
Rootless containers and user namespace mapping
domains.mastery_signal: Can pull an image, run a container with port mapping and volume mounts, generate a systemd unit file, and manage the container as a system service — all rootless

learning_objectives: Pass the RHCSA EX200 exam on the first attempt
Perform all exam tasks from memory without consulting documentation
Troubleshoot boot failures, SELinux denials, and network issues under time pressure
Configure LVM storage, file systems, and mount points that survive reboot
Manage users, groups, permissions, and sudo access with correct syntax
Configure and harden network services including SSH and firewalld
Deploy and manage containers with Podman as systemd services
Write bash scripts that handle arguments, errors, and exit codes correctly
Fix SELinux context issues and configure booleans permanently
Reset root password and recover from emergency/rescue mode

lessons.title: Shell Essentials — Navigate, Search, Redirect
lessons.summary: Master the essential tools the exam assumes you already know. Pipes, redirection, grep patterns, find expressions, and archive management. Speed matters — these commands should be muscle memory.
objectives: Chain grep, awk, and redirection to extract data from files
Use find with -name, -type, -exec, -mtime to locate files efficiently
Create and extract archives with tar, gzip, and bzip2
practice: Find all .conf files modified in the last 7 days under /etc and list them sorted by size
Extract all ERROR lines from /var/log/messages, count them, and save to a file
Create a compressed tar archive of /etc/sysconfig and verify its contents without extracting
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Given a directory with 1000 files, can find specific files by name/age/type, extract matching lines from logs, and create compressed archives — all under 5 minutes

lessons.title: Write Bash Scripts That Don't Suck
lessons.summary: The exam may ask you to write a script. It needs to work on the first run. Practice shebang lines, variables, conditionals, loops, functions, and error handling until you can write a working script from scratch in under 10 minutes.
objectives: Write scripts with proper shebang, variables, and argument handling
Use conditionals (if/test/[ ]) and loops (for/while) correctly
Handle errors with exit codes and return values
practice: Write a script that checks if a user exists, creates them if not, and reports the result
Write a script that backs up a directory with a timestamp, keeps only the last 5 backups
Write a script that monitors disk usage and alerts if any partition exceeds 80%
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can write a bash script that takes arguments, validates input, performs a task, handles errors, and exits cleanly — without looking up syntax

lessons.title: Boot Process & Systemd Targets
lessons.summary: Understand how RHEL boots from firmware to login prompt. Know the systemd target system cold — the exam WILL test your ability to change targets and troubleshoot boot failures.
objectives: Describe the RHEL boot sequence (UEFI/BIOS, GRUB2, initramfs, systemd)
Change systemd targets and set default target
Boot into rescue and emergency mode
practice: Change the default target to graphical and verify with systemctl get-default
Simulate resetting root password by adding rd.break to GRUB command line
List all available targets and explain when to use rescue vs emergency
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can reset root password via rd.break, change default boot target, and explain each stage of the boot process with specific file paths

lessons.title: systemctl & journalctl — System Control
lessons.summary: These two commands are on every RHCSA exam. Know start/stop/enable/disable/mask, and know how to filter journal output by unit, time, priority, and boot ID.
objectives: Manage services with systemctl (start, stop, enable, disable, mask, status)
Query logs with journalctl (by unit, time, priority, boot)
Configure persistent journal storage
practice: Stop and disable a service, mask it so it cannot be started, then unmask and re-enable
Find all error-level messages from the last hour across all services
Configure journald to persist logs across reboots and verify
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can manage any service's lifecycle (start/stop/enable/disable/mask) and extract specific log entries by unit, time range, and severity — instantly

lessons.title: Process Management — ps, top, kill, nice
lessons.summary: The exam tests your ability to identify, prioritize, and terminate processes. Know ps aux output columns, nice/renice values, and signal names.
objectives: List and filter processes with ps (aux, -ef, custom formats)
Adjust process priority with nice and renice
Send signals to processes (kill, killall, pkill, signal numbers)
practice: Find the process consuming the most CPU, lower its priority, and verify
Start a background process, bring it to foreground, then kill it by name
Kill all processes owned by a specific user without affecting other users
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can find any process by name/PID/user, adjust its priority, and terminate it with the correct signal — and explain why SIGTERM before SIGKILL

lessons.title: Partition Disks — MBR, GPT, fdisk, parted
lessons.summary: The exam gives you a blank disk and expects you to partition it correctly. Know fdisk for MBR and parted/GPT. Know the difference between partition types for LVM vs standard.
objectives: Create partitions with fdisk (MBR) and parted (GPT)
Set partition types (Linux, LVM, swap)
Verify partition tables with lsblk, blkid, and fdisk -l
practice: Create a 5GB LVM partition and a 2GB swap partition on a new disk using fdisk
Verify both partitions exist with lsblk and blkid
Create a GPT partition table with parted and add a 10GB partition
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can partition a new disk from scratch with both fdisk and parted, set correct partition types, and verify the result — without documentation

lessons.title: LVM — Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, Logical Volumes
lessons.summary: LVM is guaranteed on the exam. You MUST know how to create PVs, VGs, and LVs, then format, mount, and extend them. This is the single most tested storage topic.
objectives: Create and manage physical volumes (pvcreate, pvs, pvdisplay)
Create and manage volume groups (vgcreate, vgs, vgextend)
Create and extend logical volumes (lvcreate, lvs, lvextend, xfs_growfs, resize2fs)
practice: Create a PV on a new partition, create a VG, create a 2GB LV, format as xfs, mount it
Add another partition to the VG, extend the LV to 5GB, and grow the filesystem online
Create a thin-provisioned LV and verify with lvs and df
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Given a new disk, can complete the full LVM pipeline (PV → VG → LV → format → mount → fstab) and extend it later — all from memory

lessons.title: /etc/fstab & Persistent Mounts
lessons.summary: Everything must survive a reboot. Know fstab syntax cold — device/UUID, mount point, filesystem type, options, dump, pass. One wrong field and the system drops to emergency shell.
objectives: Configure /etc/fstab entries with correct syntax
Use UUID vs device path (blkid to find UUID)
Test fstab entries with mount -a before rebooting
Configure swap in fstab
key_concepts: fstab fields (device, mountpoint, type, options, dump, pass)
practice: Add an LV to fstab that mounts at /data with ext4 defaults, verify with mount -a
Configure a swap partition in fstab and activate it without rebooting
Intentionally break fstab, reboot to emergency, fix it, and recover
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can write a correct fstab entry from memory, test it safely, and recover from a broken fstab without panicking

lessons.title: Users, Groups, & sudo
lessons.summary: Create users with specific UID, home, shell, and password aging. Configure sudo access for groups. Know /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/group field formats.
objectives: Create and modify users (useradd, usermod, userdel with all flags)
Manage groups and membership (groupadd, gpasswd, usermod -aG)
Configure sudo access (/etc/sudoers, visudo, sudo log)
Set password aging policies (chage -M, -m, -W, -I, -E)
practice: Create user 'examuser' with UID 5000, home /opt/examuser, shell /bin/bash, expires 2027-01-01
Add examuser to wheel group for sudo access, verify with sudo -l
Set password aging: max 90 days, min 7 days, warn 14 days before expiry
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can create users with any combination of flags, configure sudo for groups, and set password policies — all with correct syntax from memory

lessons.title: File Permissions, Special Bits, & ACLs
lessons.summary: Basic permissions (rwx), octal notation, SUID/SGID/sticky bit, and ACLs for fine-grained access. The exam loves scenarios where you need to set up shared directories with specific access rules.
objectives: Set permissions with chmod (symbolic and octal) and ownership with chown/chgrp
Apply SUID, SGID, and sticky bit correctly
Configure ACLs (setfacl, getfacl, default ACLs, mask)
practice: Create a shared directory /project where group 'devs' can read/write/execute and new files inherit group ownership
Set ACLs so user 'audit' can read all files in /project but cannot write
Create a directory with sticky bit where users can create files but cannot delete others' files
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can set up any permission scenario from an exam prompt — shared directories, ACLs, sticky bit, SGID inheritance — with correct syntax

lessons.title: SELinux — Contexts, Booleans, & Troubleshooting
lessons.summary: SELinux is a major exam topic. You must know how to view and fix contexts, set booleans permanently, and troubleshoot denials. Most candidates fail because they disable SELinux instead of fixing it.
objectives: Check and change SELinux modes (getenforce, setenforce, /etc/selinux/config)
View and restore file contexts (ls -Z, chcon, semanage fcontext, restorecon)
Manage SELinux booleans (getsebool, setsebool -P)
Troubleshoot denials (audit2why, audit2allow, ausearch)
practice: Move Apache to a non-standard port, update SELinux to allow it, verify with curl
Fix a file context that prevents a service from reading its config, make it permanent
Find and resolve an SELinux denial from audit.log using audit2why
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Given an SELinux denial, can identify the issue from audit.log, fix the context or boolean, and make the fix permanent — without disabling SELinux

lessons.title: Firewall — firewalld Zones & Rules
lessons.summary: Configure firewalld to allow specific services and ports. Know the difference between runtime and permanent changes. The exam tests both zones and rich rules.
objectives: Manage firewall zones (firewall-cmd --list-all, --get-default-zone, --set-default-zone)
Add/remove services and ports (--add-service, --add-port, --permanent)
Create rich rules for specific source/destination/port combinations
Understand runtime vs permanent (and when to use --reload)
practice: Allow HTTP and HTTPS in the public zone permanently, reload, verify
Create a rich rule that allows SSH only from a specific subnet
Add a custom service for port 8443 and assign it to the dmz zone
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can configure any firewall scenario — services, ports, rich rules, zones — and verify the result with --list-all

lessons.title: Network Configuration with nmcli
lessons.summary: The exam uses NetworkManager. Know nmcli for connection management — show, modify, up, down, reload. Static IP, gateway, DNS, and hostname configuration.
objectives: View network configuration (nmcli device show, nmcli connection show)
Configure static IP (nmcli con mod ipv4.addresses, ipv4.gateway, ipv4.dns)
Set hostname (hostnamectl set-hostname)
Troubleshoot connectivity (ip addr, ping, ss -tlnp, dig)
key_concepts: nmcli con mod vs con edit
practice: Configure a static IP on the primary interface, set DNS and gateway, verify with ping
Change the hostname to 'rhcsa-lab' and verify with hostnamectl
Show all active connections, their IP addresses, and DNS servers
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can configure a full static IP stack (IP, gateway, DNS, hostname) using nmcli and verify connectivity — under 3 minutes

lessons.title: SSH Configuration & Key-Based Auth
lessons.summary: Configure SSH for key-based authentication, disable root login, change the default port, and restrict access by user. The exam may ask you to harden SSH.
objectives: Generate SSH key pairs (ssh-keygen, ssh-copy-id)
Configure /etc/ssh/sshd_config (PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication, AllowUsers, Port)
Restart sshd and verify changes
practice: Generate an Ed25519 key pair, copy the public key to a test user, verify key-based login
Disable root login and password authentication, allow only specific users, restart sshd
Change SSH port to 2222, update SELinux and firewalld, verify connectivity
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can set up key-based SSH auth, harden the config, and update SELinux + firewall to match — all steps verified

lessons.title: Time Synchronization — chronyd & timedatectl
lessons.summary: Time sync is critical for Kerberos, logs, and certificates. Know chronyd and timedatectl. The exam may ask you to configure a specific NTP server.
objectives: Configure time zone (timedatectl set-timezone)
Configure chronyd to use a specific NTP server (/etc/chrony.conf)
Verify time sync (chronyc sources, timedatectl show)
practice: Set the timezone to America/Chicago and verify
Configure chronyd to use a specific NTP server, restart, and verify sync
Check time synchronization status and explain the output
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can configure timezone, set up NTP with chronyd, and verify synchronization — fast and correct

lessons.title: Containers with Podman
lessons.summary: RHEL uses Podman, not Docker. The exam tests image management, container lifecycle, port mapping, volume mounts, and systemd integration. Know rootless containers.
objectives: Pull, list, inspect, tag, and remove images (podman pull, images, inspect, tag, rmi)
Run containers with port mapping and volume mounts (podman run -d -p 8080:80 -v)
Manage container lifecycle (start, stop, restart, exec, logs)
Generate systemd unit files (podman generate systemd)
Create and manage pods (podman pod create, ls, start)
practice: Pull nginx, run it on port 8080 with a volume mount, verify with curl localhost:8080
Generate a systemd unit file for the container, enable it, reboot and verify it starts
Create a pod with two containers that share a network namespace
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can deploy a container, expose it, persist it with systemd, and manage it as a service — all rootless, all from memory

lessons.title: Boot Recovery & Root Password Reset
lessons.summary: This is a GUARANTEED exam topic. You must be able to reset root password via GRUB (rd.break) and recover from a broken fstab or failed service. Practice this until you can do it in under 5 minutes.
objectives: Reset root password via rd.break on the GRUB command line
Recover from a broken /etc/fstab entry
Recover from a failed systemd service that prevents boot
practice: Reset root password via rd.break: edit GRUB, mount sysroot, chroot, passwd, touch .autorelabel
Intentionally break fstab with a bad UUID, reboot to emergency, fix it
Mask a critical service, reboot to rescue, unmask it, boot normally
lessons.mastery_checkpoint: Can reset root password and recover from boot failures — under 5 minutes, no documentation, with SELinux relabeling

practice_activities.title: Full Storage Pipeline Lab
practice_activities.prompt: You have a new 20GB disk (/dev/sdb). Complete the full pipeline: partition it as GPT with two partitions (10GB LVM, 5GB swap, rest unallocated), create PV + VG + LV named 'data-lv' (4GB), format as xfs, mount at /data persistently, activate swap, and verify everything survives a reboot. Time yourself — target under 10 minutes.

practice_activities.title: User & Sudo Configuration Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Create three users (alice, bob, charlie) with UIDs starting at 5000. Create a group 'developers' and add all three. Give alice and bob sudo access via the group. Set alice's password to expire in 30 days. Lock charlie's account. Verify sudo works for alice, fails for charlie. Target time: 5 minutes.

practice_activities.title: SELinux Troubleshooting Lab
practice_activities.prompt: A web server on port 8888 is being blocked by SELinux. Find the denial in audit.log, add the port to SELinux's allowed ports using semanage, fix any file context issues on /var/www/custom, set the httpd_can_network_connect boolean, and verify the server works with SELinux in enforcing mode. Do NOT disable SELinux.

practice_activities.title: Boot Recovery Challenge
practice_activities.prompt: Simulate exam scenario: reset the root password using rd.break. Steps: reboot, edit GRUB, add rd.break to linux line, mount sysroot rw, chroot, change password, create /.autorelabel, exit, reboot. Verify you can log in as root with the new password. Target time: 5 minutes.

practice_activities.title: Network & Firewall Configuration Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Configure a static IP (192.168.1.100/24, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 8.8.8.8) using nmcli. Set hostname to 'rhcsa-exam'. Open ports 80 and 443 in firewalld permanently. Add a rich rule allowing SSH from 192.168.1.0/24 only. Verify all changes persist across 'nmcli con reload'.

practice_activities.title: Container + Systemd Integration Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Pull the httpd image with podman. Run it rootless on port 8080 with /var/www/html mounted as a volume. Generate a systemd user service file. Enable and start it. Verify it survives a reboot (loginctl enable-linger if needed). Verify with curl localhost:8080.

practice_activities.title: Bash Scripting Challenge
practice_activities.prompt: Write a script that: accepts a username as argument, checks if the user exists, creates them if not with a random password, sets password to expire in 90 days, adds them to the 'users' group, and prints a summary. Handle errors (no argument, user already exists, etc.) with appropriate exit codes.

practice_activities.title: Fstab Disaster Recovery Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Add a bad entry to /etc/fstab (wrong UUID for a non-existent disk). Reboot. The system should drop to emergency mode. Fix fstab from the emergency shell. Reboot successfully. Then add a correct fstab entry for a real partition with the 'nofail' option so a missing disk doesn't block boot.

practice_activities.title: ACLs & Shared Directory Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Create /shared with group 'team'. Set SGID so new files inherit group. Set sticky bit so users can't delete others' files. Add ACLs: user 'auditor' gets read-only access to all current and future files. Verify: create files as different users, check permissions, confirm auditor can read but not write.

practice_activities.title: Time Sync & Timezone Lab
practice_activities.prompt: Set timezone to UTC. Configure chronyd to use pool.ntp.org. Restart chronyd. Verify sync with chronyc sources. Change timezone to America/Chicago. Verify with timedatectl. Explain why time sync matters for RHCSA (Kerberos, logs, certificates).

review_questions.q: What is the difference between systemctl enable and systemctl start?
review_questions.a: enable creates a symlink so the service starts automatically at boot. start launches the service immediately for the current session. You need both for a service that should run now AND survive reboot.

review_questions.q: How do you permanently change SELinux file context for /var/www/custom to httpd_sys_content_t?
review_questions.a: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/var/www/custom(/.*)?' then restorecon -Rv /var/www/custom. Using chcon alone is temporary and will be reset by restorecon or relabeling.

review_questions.q: What are the steps to reset a root password on RHEL 9?
review_questions.a: 1) Reboot, 2) Edit GRUB (e to edit), 3) Add rd.break to the linux line, 4) Ctrl+X to boot, 5) mount -o remount,rw /sysroot, 6) chroot /sysroot, 7) passwd root, 8) touch /.autorelabel, 9) exit twice to reboot. The autorelabel is critical — without it, SELinux locks you out again.

review_questions.q: What is the difference between xfs_growfs and resize2fs?
review_questions.a: xfs_growfs is for XFS filesystems (RHEL default). resize2fs is for ext2/3/4 filesystems. You cannot shrink XFS — only grow. ext4 can grow and shrink. Use lvextend -r to resize the LV and filesystem in one step.

review_questions.q: How do you extend an LVM logical volume and its filesystem in one command?
review_questions.a: lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vgname/lvname. The -r flag (or --resizefs) automatically resizes the underlying filesystem after extending the LV. Without -r, you must run xfs_growfs or resize2fs separately.

review_questions.q: What is the purpose of the sticky bit on a directory?
review_questions.a: The sticky bit (chmod +t or chmod 1777) prevents users from deleting or renaming files owned by other users within that directory. /tmp is the classic example — everyone can create files, but only the owner (or root) can delete them.

review_questions.q: How do you configure a service to NOT start at boot, even if another service depends on it?
review_questions.a: systemctl mask servicename. Mask creates a symlink to /dev/null, which completely prevents the service from being started manually or automatically. systemctl disable only removes the boot symlink but allows manual start.

review_questions.q: What is the correct fstab entry format and what does each field mean?
review_questions.a: Device  MountPoint  FileSystemType  Options  Dump  Pass. Example: UUID=xxx /data xfs defaults 0 0. Dump (field 5) is for backup utility (0=skip). Pass (field 6) is fsck order at boot (0=no check, 1=root, 2=other).

review_questions.q: How do you find and fix an SELinux context mismatch?
review_questions.a: 1) ls -Z to see current context, 2) matchpathcon to see expected context, 3) semanage fcontext -a -t correct_type '/path(/.*)?' to add a rule, 4) restorecon -Rv /path to apply. Check /var/log/audit/audit.log for denials if unsure what type is needed.

review_questions.q: What is the difference between firewalld runtime and permanent changes?
review_questions.a: Runtime changes take effect immediately but are lost on reboot or reload. Permanent changes are saved to config files but don't take effect until firewall-cmd --reload or --permanent is used. Best practice: use --permanent for all changes, then reload.

review_questions.q: How do you configure nmcli for a static IP?
review_questions.a: nmcli con mod 'connection-name' ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 ipv4.method manual. Then nmcli con up 'connection-name' to apply. Use ipv4.dns '+8.8.4.4' to append without replacing.

review_questions.q: What is the difference between podman and Docker for the RHCSA exam?
review_questions.a: Podman is daemonless (no background daemon), rootless by default, and uses the same CLI syntax as Docker. The exam uses Podman. Key differences: no 'dockerd', podman generate systemd for service integration, and podman pod for pod management.

review_questions.q: How do you make a Podman container start automatically at boot?
review_questions.a: Generate a systemd unit file: podman generate systemd --new --name container-name > /etc/systemd/system/container-name.service. Then systemctl daemon-reload, systemctl enable container-name. For rootless containers, use loginctl enable-linger for the user.

review_questions.q: What does 'touch /.autorelabel' do after resetting root password?
review_questions.a: It tells SELinux to relabel the entire filesystem on the next boot. After chroot and passwd, the /etc/shadow file gets new content with incorrect SELinux context. Without the relabel, SELinux in enforcing mode blocks login even with the correct password.

review_questions.q: How do you configure persistent journal storage in systemd?
review_questions.a: Create /var/log/journal directory: mkdir -p /var/log/journal. Then restart journald: systemctl restart systemd-journald. By default, journald uses volatile storage (/run/log/journal). Creating the persistent directory switches to persistent storage that survives reboot.
